The English poet William Blake (1790) asserts the counterintuitive notion that “If the fool would persist in his folly he would become wise” (p. 7). This may strike us as a decidedly modern psychoanalytic formulation, exemplified in techniques such as joining and following the contact function. When one is free to fully explore the nature and substance of one's personal folly or delusion, Blake and modern psychoanalysts seem to suggest, one is bound to exhaust the delusion's potency and its efficacy as a defense against reality. The Argentinian-born Parisian psychoanalyst Salomon Resnik harmonizes with Blake in his recent book, The Logics of Madness: On Infantile and Delusional Transference. Indeed, R. D. Laing, whom Resnik quotes, all but echoes Blake when he suggests that “madness need not be all breakdown. It may also be breakthrough.” However, Resnik is careful to go beyond Blake's sentiment to reject the implication that his patients are “fools,” reminding the reader that “the intimacy of very disturbed people who have lost at least part of their own identity demands an approach that is highly respectful.” And he cites Wilfred Bion for the idea that “complete madness does not exist as such. Some part of the personality is always preserved, and the analytic process can enable us to get in touch with it and to work through the psychotic aspects.

Jane Goldberg

Jane Goldberg

Jane Goldberg  

Claudia Luiz's book is arguably the best lay book written on modern psychoanalysis. The author is very much a professional, but she writes here in language that will be easily understood by anyone, and she tells stories of her work with patients in a compelling way that would be equally interesting to analysts and to

190

laypeople. And this lay book's power and poignancy are such that this reviewer, a quite seasoned clinician (45 years of seeing patients), not only thoroughly enjoyed it but, more importantly, learned from it. It incorporates autobiographical reflections at times, both sensitive and tactful, that have the effect of presenting the reader with an openhearted account of her own growth, as a woman, a wife, a mother, and an analyst.

Luiz's writing reveals all the basic attributes of a qualified, talented clinician: she is smart, sensitive, astute, intuitive. But what struck me especially clearly, shining through every sentence and every thought, was her training. She had the same training I had (essentially, though most of hers was at CMPS's sister institute in Boston), and constantly as I read, on practically every page, there was a recognition moment for me—an intellectual and emotional perception of the theoretical perspective we share. This is not to say that all the aforementioned attributes are not equally important as training—intuition, empathy, intelligence are clearly invaluable, even essential qualities; but they are not all. Good training brings talented analysts to be, as Luiz clearly is, brilliantly effective analysts.

Luiz illustrates, through many vignettes of her work with patients, the conceptualization of how to effectively be with patients. Of course, this concept of being with the patient is definitional to the work analysts do. We must approach the work essentially without ambition: no wish to change the patient, no wish to take them out of pain, no wish for anything at all to happen in the treatment other than finding ways of being together. And this assumption, although never stated explicitly, permeates Luiz's book, making it to my mind the best advertisement for modern analysis yet created. The book is imbued with what is clearly an absolute love affair with her experiences as an analysand and her modern analytic training, in classes, in groups, in supervision; and subsequent to all that, the persistence of her curiosity and pleasure in growing as she developed and refined her own ways of applying with her patients the theories and techniques of Spotnitz and his trainees and successors.

Based on non-linear dynamical fractal theory, the author proposes that humans benefit from interactions with natural (fractal) phenomena. In the process, he shows that the interaction between two fractally similar humans produces synchrony, a dynamic process that characterizes useful therapeutic relationships. Because synchrony, as defined in this article, crosses many scientific and artistic domains, it is seen as a unifying concept that supports, along with a broader spectrum of concepts, the importance of several modern psychoanalytic techniques and reinforces the significance of emotional communication.

This condescending and attacking behavior went on for a long time and seemed to have the intention of debasing me, while simultaneously keeping me looking at him, although from the position of an unsatisfactory wounded supplicant, dependent, admiring and envious—reflection of his own maternal rejection and its consequences.

John Madonna, p. 67

Maintaining emotional presence in psychoanalysis is no simple task. Not only does this presence act as the conduit between the unconscious of the analyst and that of the patient, but at times, the irrational, or perhaps erratic, swirling of these currents between minds can play tricks on us. We are drawn into the internal processes of the other without much warning: suddenly touched by an unknown, often frightening reality, we also have to contend with the deep fissures of our own mind. It can feel like a hijacking, or sometimes a slow, seductive movement, a pushing-away and pulling-toward, seemingly exposing one's most protected vulnerability by its uninvited illumination. As we hold up a mirror to the patient, they do the same to us: in our mutual yet separate reflections we find ourselves within the confusing and shifting landscape of who we were, who we are at that moment, and who we might become in an unknowable future. Paradoxically, we need to let go of ourselves in order for a state of being fully present to emerge.

The author examines Winnicott's “fear of breakdown” idea as it may relate to the transmission of trauma and to the question of psychosis, and to its manifestation in the transference. Winnicott, at the end of his paper, turned his formulation around and spoke of nothing happening, when something could have happened. Dr. Fromm asks whether this tragically empty moment might speak to the fear of breakthrough that both parent and child sense as they stumble into the fallout of trauma that one has been carrying for the other.

Galit Atlas   Faculty at the postdoctoral program in psychotherapy and psychoanalysis at New York University, and faculty in the four-year adult and national training programs at National Institute for the Psychotherapies. She is the author of The Enigma of Desire: Sex, Longing and Belonging in Psychoanalysis and, with Lewis Aron, of Dramatic Dialogue: Contemporary Clinical Practice. Atlas serves on the editorial board of Psychoanalytic Perspectives and writes on gender and sexuality. She is a psychoanalyst and clinical supervisor in private practice in New York City.

The author's presentation, based on her book The Enigma of Desire, reexamines Winnicott's “Fear of Breakdown” in the context of what she terms breaks in unity, the undertheorized realm of the maternal body, and the complex relationship between birth and loss. She proposes that an inherent part of the process of motherhood includes an existential break: a break of physical and emotional boundaries, a break of meaning, a break of continuity, and therefore a break of the unity of the self. These processes are integral but often unspoken dimensions of childbirth and motherhood. Exploring the realm of the maternal body, she considers the nature of development and psychopathology as they relate to early maternal development, infant-mother boundaries, and unconscious communication.

Psychoanalysis as effective, practical help for troubled humans (all of us, isn't it?) and also as a science of human nature, is, goodness knows, all too often portrayed in popular media as archaic or precious or both, and in any case best left to those who have both years and unlimited funds to spend on the self-indulgent endeavor of talking about themselves. To make matters worse, managed care agencies (“CBT vultures,” a friend recently characterized some of them that were offering jobs to her medical students) are descending on recent graduates of mental health disciplines across the board, threatening to push psychoanalysis even further toward the fringes of currently adopted treatment modalities.

These realities make even more imperative the need for psychoanalysts to do more writing for the general public, and to generate not only as much understanding as possible of analysis, but as a result of that, a desire to engage with it. To that end, Jane Goldberg's most recent work, My Mother, My Daughter, My Self, is an important book. Along with the pleasure to be had from it for any reader, practitioners should read it as a model for how this kind of writing can successfully be done.

Explaining—often one's first impulse—is not the answer. For a book to take root and make a difference, the psychoanalytic author must succeed at arousing real feelings in the reader, and thereby induce a more than intellectual, indeed almost physical desire to think more “analytically.” And crucial to that effort will be to find new words to be used for such age-old concepts as, for example, “regression” or “unconscious,” that will save the writing from becoming pedantic—too intellectual, too “inside,” so that the reader can engage with the story and have an emotional experience. As I will now venture to show you, Goldberg has achieved both goals.

Goldberg's book, written in three parts, takes us simultaneously deeper and deeper into both psychoanalysis and her own mind, like an unfolding mystery. The first and shortest section, “My Mother,” begins with a broad-sweeping character analysis of her mother.

When the Sun Bursts: The Enigma of Schizophrenia. Christopher Bollas. New Haven, CT and London: Yale University Press, 2015. 226 pp.

Joseph Scalia

Joseph Scalia

Joseph Scalia  

Christopher Bollas's (2015) When the Sun Bursts: The Enigma of Schizophrenia presents a significant opportunity for psychoanalysis and for what psychoanalysis has to offer the world. It can be read as a call to arms for psychoanalysts, whatever our points of disagreement among ourselves. Bollas's writing has been read widely, both within and outside of the profession; it provides, then, an unusually broad dissemination of psychoanalysis as the treatment of choice for psychotics, as the author considers it to be. In these days of “evidence-based” therapies, whereby evidence is recognized and defined by health insurance and pharmaceutical interests, Bollas provides a welcome, readable and humanizing approach to a patient population that is all too commonly technocratically objectified. It offers evidence of what humane and respectful reception and treatment of the psychotic subject can be. It offers scholarly and psychoanalytical evidence of what treatment of the psychotic—and the anorectic1, whom the author several times parenthetically compares with the psychotic—might be in a world beyond scientism's rendering of everything in metrics and economics.

An overarching observation one ought to register about this new book is of its effort, like much of Bollas's oeuvre, to assimilate a variety of psychoanalytic schools and traditions that typically come only as close as, say, ships of several different navies in the same sea—prominently including modern psychoanalytic, Lacanian, and Bionian. Any such effort itself must be delimited and limited, as well as unique to its author (Ogden and Gabbard, 2016). Psychoanalysis, dealing as it does with the complex nature of the human mind, with the elusive human being, is regularly prompted to carefully consult bodies of thought too

1Bollas doesn't develop the point in the book, but he does point out in brief mentions here and there certain similarities between the psychotic and the anorectic. What I take from these comments is his proposal, which is also present in his (1999) book Hysteria, that the anorectic has, as much as the psychotic, been rejected by the dominant mental health ideology and discourse as not suited to psychoanalysis, when psychoanalysis, actually, can be argued to be its treatment of choice.

She has written and presented numerous papers on adolescent treatment, emotional communication, dreams, education, and psychoanalytic perspectives of literary characters and their authors. Ethical Challenges and Considerations in the Treatment of Children

Virginia Elliott LMHC

Virginia Elliott

1581 Beacon St.
Brookline, MA 02446
email: elliottv@bgsp.edu

Virginia Elliott   Faculty of BGSP where she serves on advisement and school-internship committees. She has presented on clinical work with children in the schools. She is in private practice in Brookline, MA and works with children in the Boston public schools.

This paper outlines areas of ethical concern in psychoanalytic treatment, such as confidentiality, countertransference, and boundaries, when working with children, noting where proceedings could ethically come into question. It is not necessarily focused on rules, or a code that is suitable for analytic work with children, but with the psychoanalytic ethic which is best for a child. The treatment of children presents issues that can become ethical ones unless there is an understanding of how feelings and behaviors aroused in working with the young can affect the clinician.
